original_question: Does every Seidel matrix with exactly three distinct rational eigenvalues contain a regular graph in its switching class?
target_in_paper: Problem 3.34 in Section 3.8 ("Seidel matrices") of arXiv:1907.04349; the survey explicitly says this related problem also appears in Greaves [44].
correct_elements: Your draft matches the paper's official formulation almost verbatim: it asks about every Seidel matrix, requires precisely/exactly three distinct rational eigenvalues, and asks whether the switching class contains a regular graph. The only real gap is that it is not fully stand-alone, because the paper's surrounding context supplies what a Seidel matrix is and what 'switching class' means.
missing_details: Specify that the Seidel matrix is the Seidel matrix of a finite simple graph, i.e. S(G) = J - I - 2A(G).

Spell out that 'switching class' means Seidel switching: equivalently, matrices of the form DSD where D is diagonal with diagonal entries ±1 (and, at the graph level, the corresponding switched graphs).
Clarify that 'rational eigenvalues' means all three distinct eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix are rational numbers.
Clarify that 'contain a regular graph' means there exists at least one regular graph in that Seidel switching class.
refined_question: Let G be a finite simple graph, and let S(G) = J - I - 2A(G) be its Seidel matrix. If S(G) has precisely three distinct eigenvalues and all three are rational numbers, must there exist a regular graph H such that S(H) = D S(G) D for some diagonal matrix D with diagonal entries in {±1}?
justification: In the provided paper, the nearest official formulation is Problem 3.34, which is exactly your draft question up to the word choice 'exactly' versus 'precisely'. The nearby context needed to make it self-contained is spread across the introduction, where switching is defined, and Section 3.1/3.8, where Seidel matrices are identified with signed complete graphs and Seidel switching is explained. The surrounding discussion in Section 3.8 also shows that this problem is intentionally narrower than the adjacent Problem 3.33: the rationality restriction is part of the paper's intent, not an accidental omission, because the authors immediately discuss nonrational-eigenvalue examples as motivation for asking the rational version separately.
